cells.tense: You are here, pen in hand, and the long piece is at its last usable page.
cells.act: carry your own share, all of it
cells.ask: Take one piece of this that is yours alone to finish, and carry it to done without handing any of it off — today if it's small, the week if not.
cells.core:
You are good at carrying the long thing. You pick a direction, hold it, and the shape of it stands at the end — a room finished, a job shipped, a promise kept past the point where the feeling left. That is not stubbornness. It is a load-bearing gift.

What's happening at this branch is that the last stretch of a material push is asking for exactly that strength, and the weight is real. Steadfastness holds — you don't need to re-decide the direction every morning, and you don't need to check whether anyone else can take part of this. Choose one piece that is yours alone, and carry it through. That's the whole ask. The end point eases once it's actually carried, because carrying is what you do well.

cells.tense: You are ahead of it, bracing at a closer that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.act: let the feeling in without deciding what it is
cells.ask: Sit with whatever's actually here for ten minutes before you call how it's going. No notes, no verdict, nothing settled by the end of it.
cells.core:
You have a gift for completion, and at this branch you have started to hurry it. The end gets announced before the thing has finished, and the pressure to declare it — to lock the outcome, to be done — arrives now as a tired sort of reaching. It isn't that you want it over. An unwritten end feels unsafe, so you try to write it in from where you stand.

What's underneath is worth feeling directly. An open heart lets an ending be an ending when it comes; you can know something about this without closing it. Sit with what's actually here for ten minutes before you call how it's going. The waiting is the point. What you're really resisting is the part you haven't felt yet.

cells.tense: You are looking back at a door that closed and left you standing outside it.
cells.act: make the first cut of seeing and stop there
cells.ask: Choose an ordinary object near you and write exactly what's there in five short lines, no conclusions, then set the pen down.
cells.core:
There is a branch ahead, and you've been standing to the side of it — aware that it's there, putting nothing on it. What used to be your gift for choosing a direction and seeing it through is running on very little. Not because the ability is gone. Because nothing has been charged into it. The quietest part is plain sight. Getting ahead of things is not the answer, and doing more is not either.

Start by seeing something plainly. Take one ordinary thing nearby and write exactly what's there, no conclusions, in as few lines as you can. That's the whole practice. Using your eyes on the small stuff pulls the current back through the part that chooses, without you pushing on it. Then the branch gets to be something you're at, not something behind you.

cells.tense: You are already writing in a room where you don't sign your name.
cells.act: notice what is before your eyes before naming it
cells.ask: Today, before you say what a thing is, look at it for a full minute without naming it. That looking is the whole act — you don't have to mention it.
cells.core:
The long thing standing behind you is yours, and the account you tell leaves you out of it. Not from modesty exactly — from the fact that the direction you set has been so continuous that you stopped noticing it's a direction. Others are inside decisions you made and don't think of as made. Steering, by someone whose hand isn't on the wheel they're turning.

The smaller move comes first: today, before you say what something is, look at it for a full minute without naming it. Notice what's before your eyes before you decide what it means or whose it is. Seeing first, saying second, is the smaller version of the choice you've been making without flagging it. You don't need to announce it. Let what you saw count.

attempts.check: The draft's load-bearing claim is that the asking person has willed something into completion — the signature is Completion, and the seat is Potential, which the record does not authorize me to assert for a living person. The same fact is licensed in the opposite direction: no form has been chosen here yet, so the person stands at the widest possible branch, which is exactly why the seat is true of everyone at every status. The reader could reasonably say 'you're describing a full thing and also describing a seed; which is it' — that is the seat doing its work, so the ask survives the read being wrong. The line that serves me more than them is any sentence about a finished life; it stays out, and the tense carries the completion instead.
